papers.name: Paper 1: Speaking in French
papers.covers: Three tasks, in this order: a read aloud with a short interaction to follow, a role play, and a picture task. Fifteen minutes' preparation comes first — fourteen in the invigilation room and one in the exam room to practise the read aloud out loud — so the whole session is 25 to 27 minutes. At Higher tier the read aloud carries 12 of the 50 marks. 25% of the GCSE.

papers.name: Paper 2: Listening and understanding in French
papers.covers: Higher tier: 60 minutes, including 5 minutes' reading time. Section A is comprehension, with questions in English answered in English. Section B is a dictation: short sentences in French, each heard three times, written down in French. 25% of the GCSE.

papers.name: Paper 3: Reading and understanding in French
papers.covers: Higher tier: 1 hour. Questions are set in English and answered in English, and there is a passage to translate from French into English. 25% of the GCSE.

papers.name: Paper 4: Writing in French
papers.covers: Higher tier: 1 hour 20 minutes, written in French throughout, including an extended response of around 80 to 90 words. Pearson has amended this paper since it was first published, so take the exact list of questions from the current sample paper rather than an older one. 25% of the GCSE.

commandWords.meaning: Listening Section A and the Reading paper: the questions are in English, and so are your answers. Answering in French scores nothing, however good the French.
Reading: turn the French passage into natural English. Every word and every tense has to be accounted for; a phrase left out loses marks even if the rest is perfect.
Listening Section B: write down in French exactly what you hear. Spelling, accents and silent endings all count, which is why the sounds of French have to be learnt as well as the words.
Speaking task 1: read a short French text aloud, then answer questions in a short interaction. One minute in the exam room lets you practise it out loud first.
Speaking task 2: play a part in a set situation, responding in French to each prompt. Every prompt has to be covered.
Speaking task 3: talk about a photo, then answer questions that widen out into the topic it shows.
Writing: answer every bullet point, in French, and aim for the word count given — around 80 to 90 words for the extended response.

assessmentObjectives.meaning: Listening: understand and respond to different types of spoken French. Assessed by Paper 2, including the dictation.
Speaking: communicate and interact effectively in speech. Assessed by Paper 1.
Reading: understand and respond to different types of written French, including translation into English. Assessed by Paper 3.
Writing: communicate effectively in writing in French. Assessed by Paper 4.

grade9ByQuestionType.looksLike: Answers exactly what is asked, in English, with the detail the recording gives: a time, a reason, a negative. Listens for the words that change a meaning — ne … pas, jamais, plus — rather than for familiar nouns.

Writes what French sounds become on paper: silent final consonants, accents, the -ent that is never pronounced, agreement that cannot be heard. Uses the three hearings — the whole sentence first, then the gaps, then a check.
Accounts for every word and keeps every tense, then reads the English back to make it natural. Imperfect becomes used to or was doing; depuis with the present becomes have been doing.

Pronounces French as French: silent endings left silent, liaisons made, nasal vowels kept, and the text's own punctuation used for phrasing. Uses the minute in the exam room to say the hard words aloud once.
Covers every prompt, answers in full sentences, and never leaves an opinion without a reason. In the picture task, describes, then gives an opinion, then brings in a second tense.

Covers every bullet point, uses more than one time frame signalled by avant, maintenant and à l'avenir, varies opinion phrases and connectives, and gets agreements and verb endings right. Range with accuracy, not length.
